entry.title: Computer-aided Lyapunov analyses in optimization
entry.content:
Many convergence proofs for first-order methods in optimization follow a common pattern: construct a Lyapunov function, establish an inequality describing its decrease, and use this inequality to show that a performance measure converges to zero. Within many standard problem classes and prescribed families of Lyapunov functions, these tasks can often be formulated exactly as semidefinite programs (SDPs). Existing solvers can then be used to search numerically for feasible solutions. Convergence analysis itself thus becomes a tractable optimization problem.

Closely related is the performance estimation problem (PEP) methodology, introduced by Drori and Teboulle [DT14]. For many first-order methods and problem classes, the search for a worst-case example can be reformulated as an SDP, giving tight worst-case guarantees [THG17]. The standard PEP methodology is now a mature technology for worst-case analysis, supported by software packages such as PEPit [GMG+24].

However, standard PEP formulations analyze a fixed number of iterations, with the number of variables and constraints typically growing quadratically with this horizon. Deriving closed-form guarantees valid for all iterations can also be challenging. Automated Lyapunov analyses provide a complementary approach: restricting the search to prescribed families of Lyapunov analyses can give smaller SDPs whose number of variables and constraints is independent of the iteration horizon, or grows only linearly with it, facilitating concise, closed-form convergence proofs [TVSL18, TB19, UBTG25, UDGT+26]. A closely related framework uses integral quadratic constraints (IQCs), developed in robust control [MR97], to obtain convergence guarantees through linear matrix inequalities (LMIs) that can be checked by semidefinite programming [LRP16, MSE21]. Although searching over prescribed families of Lyapunov functions may give conservative bounds, these bounds can still match the actual worst-case behavior in many settings.

In this post, we derive the corresponding SDPs explicitly for two examples: an inexact gradient method, for which the Lyapunov function is fixed in advance, and a gradient method with memory, for which we search for a Lyapunov function within a prescribed family. The aim is to explain the main ideas in a simple setting and provide a starting point for analyses of other methods and problem classes. For the first example, we also show how to extract a closed-form proof of a tight convergence guarantee from numerical SDP solutions. In the second example, we show how allowing a more flexible class of Lyapunov functions can give tighter convergence guarantees. This post assumes familiarity with smooth and strongly convex optimization, basic matrix algebra, and Lagrangian duality. On a first reading, the expandable derivations and proofs can be skipped.

1. Problem setting

For simplicity, both examples use the familiar setting of smooth and strongly convex optimization, although the tools developed here apply more broadly. We consider the unconstrained problem

egin{equation} \label{eq:optimization-problem} \mathop{ ext{minimize}}\limits_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d}\; f(x) \end{equation}

where \(f:\mathbb{R}^d o\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable, has an \(L\)-Lipschitz continuous gradient (that is, \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth), and is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, with \(0<\mu<L\). We denote this class of functions by \(\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Equivalently, \(f\) satisfies

egin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-bounds} ( orall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d})\qquad \left[ egin{aligned} f(x) &\leqslant f(y)+\langle abla f(y),x-y angle + frac{L}{2}\lVert x-y Vert^{2},\ f(x) &\geqslant f(y)+\langle abla f(y),x-y angle + frac{\mu}{2}\lVert x-y Vert^{2}, \end{aligned} ight. \end{equation}

where \(\langle\cdot,\cdot angle\) is the Euclidean inner product and \(\lVert\cdot Vert\) is its induced norm. For the quadratic bounds above, see [Bec17, Theorems 5.8(ii) and 5.24(ii)]. Strong convexity ensures that problem \(\eqref{eq:optimization-problem}\) has a unique minimizer \(x^\star\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\), characterized by \( abla f(x^\star)=0\) [Bec17, Theorems 3.63 and 5.25(a)]. Figure 1 illustrates these inequalities geometrically, showing how \(f\) is globally bounded above and below by quadratic functions tangent to it at any chosen point.

2. Fixed Lyapunov functions

Here we check a Lyapunov function chosen in advance, then use the tools developed here to search for one in Section 3.

2.1 The gradient method with inexact gradients

The standard gradient method provides a familiar starting point; here, we consider a slightly richer variant with inexact gradients. Given a constant step size \(\gamma>0\) and an initial point \(x^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\), consider

egin{equation} \label{eq:relatively-inexact-gradient-method} \left[ egin{aligned} & ext{Pick }d^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\; ext{such that}\; \| abla f(x^{k}) - d^{k}\| \leqslant \varepsilon \| abla f(x^{k})\|,\ &x^{k+1} = x^{k} - \gamma d^{k}, \end{aligned} ight. \end{equation}

where \(\varepsilon\in[0,1)\) bounds the relative error in the gradient approximation. We seek convergence guarantees that hold for every sequence of approximations \(d^k\) satisfying this bound. When \(\varepsilon=0\), we recover the standard gradient method.

2.2 Lyapunov functions and contraction

To quantify convergence, we track a nonnegative scalar quantity such as squared distance to the solution \(\|x^{k}-x^{\star}\|^2\) or function-value suboptimality \(f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star})\). We call such a quantity a performance measure. Under the standing assumptions, it is natural to seek bounds of the form

egin{equation} \label{eq:contraction-examples} \|x^{k+1}-x^{\star}\|^2 \leqslant ho_{\mathtt{norm}^2}(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L)\|x^{k}-x^{\star}\|^2 \quad ext{or}\quad f(x^{k+1})-f(x^{\star}) \leqslant ho_{\mathtt{func}}(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L)(f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star})), \end{equation}

and to determine which choices of \(\gamma\) ensure that the corresponding factors satisfy

egin{equation*} 0\leqslant ho_{\mathtt{norm}^2}(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L) < 1 \quad ext{and}\quad 0\leqslant ho_{\mathtt{func}}(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L) < 1. \end{equation*}

In these examples, we use the performance measure itself as a Lyapunov function, establishing convergence by proving a contraction inequality for that same quantity. More generally, we consider nonnegative and nontrivial Lyapunov functions \(\mathcal{V}\) satisfying

egin{equation} \label{eq:lyapunov-contraction} \mathcal{V}(k+1) \leqslant ho(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L)\mathcal{V}(k), \end{equation}

and seek conditions ensuring \(0\leqslant ho(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L)<1\). Iterating the contraction inequality \eqref{eq:lyapunov-contraction} gives

egin{equation*} \mathcal{V}(k)\leqslant ho(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L)^{k}\mathcal{V}(0) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal{V}(k)\in\mathcal{O}( ho(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L)^{k}) \quad ext{as}\quad k o\infty, \end{equation*}

and we say that \(\mathcal{V}\) converges linearly to zero with rate at most \( ho(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L)\). In particular, we seek the smallest factor for which \eqref{eq:lyapunov-contraction} holds.

We build on squared distance \(\|x^{k}-x^{\star}\|^2\) and function-value suboptimality \(f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star})\) in \(\eqref{eq:contraction-examples}\) by also using gradient information. Including the squared gradient norm \(\| abla f(x^{k})\|^2\) and the inner product \(\langle x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}) angle\) allows us to account for the gradient’s magnitude and its alignment with \(x^{k}-x^{\star}\). We therefore consider the family

egin{align*} \mathcal{V}(k) &= Q_{1,1} orm{x^{k}-x^{\star}}^{2} +2Q_{1,2}\inner{x^{k}-x^{\star}}{ abla f(x^{k})} +Q_{2,2} orm{ abla f(x^{k})}^{2} +q(f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star})), \end{align*}

where \(Q=(Q_{i,j})_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant2}\in\mathbb{R}^{2 imes2}\) is symmetric and \(q\in\mathbb{R}\).

For fixed \(Q\) and \(q\), \(\mathcal{V}\) is linear in the squared norms, inner products, and function-value differences that become variables of the SDP derived in Section 2.3. More general mixed terms need not admit a linear representation in those variables. For that derivation, we group the two vectors \(x^{k}-x^{\star}\) and \( abla f(x^{k})\) and write

egin{align*} \mathcal{V}(k) &= \inner{(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}))}{(Q \otimes I_{d})(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}))} + q(f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star})), \end{align*}

where \(\otimes\) is the Kronecker product and \(I_{d}\) is the identity matrix in \(\mathbb{R}^{d imes d}\).

Here, we fix \(Q\) and \(q\) so that \(\mathcal{V}\) is nonnegative and nontrivial. The two cases in \(\eqref{eq:contraction-examples}\) correspond to

egin{align} \label{eq:lyapunov-examples} \mathcal{V}(k) &= egin{cases} orm{x^{k}-x^{\star}}^{2}, & ext{if } Q=\mathord{ egin{bmatrix}1&0\0&0\end{bmatrix}}\; ext{and}\; q=0,\[0.5em] f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star}), & ext{if } Q=0\; ext{and}\; q=1. \end{cases} \end{align}
2.3 Optimal contraction via semidefinite programming

To verify \(\eqref{eq:lyapunov-contraction}\) along every trajectory, it suffices to consider one step from an arbitrary point \(x^{k}\). The update rule and the coefficients \(Q\) and \(q\) are the same at every iteration, and any such step can be realized as the first step by setting \(x^{0}=x^{k}\). We therefore define the optimal one-step contraction factor by

egin{equation*} ho_d^{\star}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L) =\inf\left\{ ho\in\mathbb{R}\;\middle|\; egin{array}{l} \mathcal{V}(k+1)\leqslant ho\mathcal{V}(k)\ ext{for every }f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) \; ext{and}\; x^{k},d^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} ext{ with}\ x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k}\quad ext{and}\quad \| abla f(x^{k})-d^{k}\|\leqslant\varepsilon\| abla f(x^{k})\| \end{array} ight\}. \end{equation*}

We will show, step by step, how semidefinite programming gives an upper bound on this quantity and under which conditions the bound equals the optimal one-step contraction factor. We first fix a candidate \( ho\) and derive a semidefinite feasibility test, then minimize \( ho\) in this test. This feasibility formulation will also let us search for valid Lyapunov functions in Section 3, where their coefficients become additional variables.

Worst-case Lyapunov difference. For a fixed candidate \( ho\), we maximize the difference \(\mathcal{V}(k+1)- ho\mathcal{V}(k)\) over all admissible functions and updates:

egin{equation*} \mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L, ho) = \left( egin{array}{cl} \mathop{ ext{maximize}}\limits_{\substack{ f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\ x^{k},x^{k+1},x^{\star},d^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} }} & \mathcal{V}(k+1)- ho\,\mathcal{V}(k)\[0.3em] ext{subject to} & x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k},\ & orm{ abla f(x^{k})-d^{k}}\leqslant\varepsilon orm{ abla f(x^{k})},\ & abla f(x^{\star})=0 \end{array} ight). \end{equation*}

The contraction inequality \(\eqref{eq:lyapunov-contraction}\) holds for every admissible function and update exactly when \(\mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L, ho)\leqslant0\). The optimal one-step contraction factor is therefore

egin{equation*} ho_d^{\star}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L) =\inf\{ ho\in\mathbb{R}\mid\mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L, ho)\leqslant0\}. \end{equation*}

We next derive a semidefinite test for the condition \(\mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L, ho)\leqslant0\). We will describe the possible function values and gradients using finitely many inequalities, collect vector inner products in a positive semidefinite matrix, and combine these inequalities to certify contraction.

Encoding inner products with a Gram matrix. Before we proceed, we introduce some convenient notation. Let \(\mathbb{S}^{n}\) and \(\mathbb{S}_{+}^{n}\) denote the sets of real-valued symmetric and positive semidefinite \(n imes n\) matrices, respectively. We define the Gramian function \(\mathtt{Gram}:(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n} o\mathbb{S}^{n}_{+}\) by

egin{align*} ( orall \mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\in(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}) \qquad \mathtt{Gram}(\mathbf{z}) = (\inner{z_i}{z_j})_{1\leqslant i,j \leqslant n}. \end{align*}

In particular, \((\mathtt{Gram}(\mathbf{z}))_{i,i}= orm{z_i}^{2}\), so squared norms appear as diagonal entries. With this, we can write the Lyapunov function as

egin{align*} \mathcal{V}(k) = ext{trace}(Q\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star} , abla f(x^{k}))) + q(f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star})). \end{align*}

For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m imes n}\), \(M\in\mathbb{S}^{m}\), and \(\mathbf{z}\in(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}\), we will use the identities

egin{equation} \label{eq:gram-trace-identities} egin{aligned} \mathtt{Gram}((A\otimes I_d)\mathbf{z}) &=A\,\mathtt{Gram}(\mathbf{z})A^{ op},\ ext{trace} igl(M\,\mathtt{Gram}((A\otimes I_d)\mathbf{z}) igr) &= ext{trace} igl(A^{ op}MA\,\mathtt{Gram}(\mathbf{z}) igr). \end{aligned} \end{equation}
Show proofHide proof

For each \(1\leqslant i,j\leqslant m\), bilinearity of the inner product gives

egin{align*} (\mathtt{Gram}((A\otimes I_d)\mathbf{z}))_{i,j} &=\Biginner{\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}A_{i,\ell}z_{\ell}}{\sum_{r=1}^{n}A_{j,r}z_r}\ &=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}A_{i,\ell}A_{j,r}\inner{z_{\ell}}{z_r}\ &=(A\,\mathtt{Gram}(\mathbf{z})A^{ op})_{i,j}. \end{align*}

Substituting this identity and using cyclicity of the trace gives

egin{align*} ext{trace} igl(M\,\mathtt{Gram}((A\otimes I_d)\mathbf{z}) igr) &= ext{trace} igl(MA\,\mathtt{Gram}(\mathbf{z})A^{ op} igr)\ &= ext{trace} igl(A^{ op}MA\,\mathtt{Gram}(\mathbf{z}) igr). \end{align*}

Rewriting the objective. Our goal is to express the objective of \(\mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L, ho)\) in terms of the function-value differences \(f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star})\) and \(f(x^{k+1})-f(x^{\star})\), together with the Gram matrix \(\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}), abla f(x^{k+1}),d^{k})\). For this purpose, we introduce the following matrices, whose columns correspond, from left to right, to the four arguments of this Gramian:

egin{equation*} S= egin{bmatrix} 1&0&0&0\ 0&1&0&0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad S_+= egin{bmatrix} 1&0&0&-\gamma\ 0&0&1&\phantom{-}0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{equation*}

Applying the trace identity in \(\eqref{eq:gram-trace-identities}\) with these matrices gives the objective in the desired form

egin{equation*} \mathcal{V}(k+1)- ho\mathcal{V}(k) = ext{trace} igl((S_+^{ op}QS_+- ho S^{ op}QS)\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}), abla f(x^{k+1}),d^{k}) igr) +q egin{bmatrix}- ho\\phantom{-}1\end{bmatrix}^{ op} egin{bmatrix} f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star})\ f(x^{k+1})-f(x^{\star}) \end{bmatrix}. \end{equation*}
Show proofHide proof

The map \(S\otimes I_d\) selects \(x^{k}-x^{\star}\) and \( abla f(x^{k})\), the two vectors in the Gramian term of \(\mathcal{V}(k)\), giving

egin{equation*} (S\otimes I_d)(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}), abla f(x^{k+1}),d^{k}) =(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k})). \end{equation*}

For \(\mathcal{V}(k+1)\), the map \(S_+\otimes I_d\) recovers \(x^{k+1}-x^{\star}\) and \( abla f(x^{k+1})\) using the update \(x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k}\), giving

egin{equation*} (S_+\otimes I_d)(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}), abla f(x^{k+1}),d^{k}) =(x^{k}-x^{\star}-\gamma d^{k}, abla f(x^{k+1})) =(x^{k+1}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k+1})). \end{equation*}

Applying the trace identity in \(\eqref{eq:gram-trace-identities}\) gives

egin{align*} \mathcal{V}(k) &= ext{trace} igl(Q\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k})) igr)+q(f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star}))\ &= ext{trace} igl(Q\,\mathtt{Gram}((S\otimes I_d)(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}), abla f(x^{k+1}),d^{k})) igr)+q(f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star}))\ &= ext{trace} igl(S^{ op}QS\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}), abla f(x^{k+1}),d^{k}) igr)+q(f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star})). \end{align*}

Similarly, we obtain

egin{align*} \mathcal{V}(k+1) &= ext{trace} igl(Q\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k+1}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k+1})) igr)+q(f(x^{k+1})-f(x^{\star}))\ &= ext{trace} igl(Q\,\mathtt{Gram}((S_+\otimes I_d)(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}), abla f(x^{k+1}),d^{k})) igr)+q(f(x^{k+1})-f(x^{\star}))\ &= ext{trace} igl(S_+^{ op}QS_+\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}), abla f(x^{k+1}),d^{k}) igr)+q(f(x^{k+1})-f(x^{\star})). \end{align*}

Subtracting \( ho\mathcal{V}(k)\) from \(\mathcal{V}(k+1)\) gives the stated expression.

Optimizing over functions. Using this trace representation of the objective gives the following equivalent formulation of the problem defining \(\mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L, ho)\)

egin{equation*} egin{array}{cl} \mathop{ ext{maximize}}\limits_{\substack{ f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\ x^{k},x^{k+1},x^{\star},d^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} }} & ext{trace}((S_+^{ op}QS_+- ho S^{ op}QS)\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star}, abla f(x^{k}), abla f(x^{k+1}),d^{k})) +q egin{bmatrix}- ho\\phantom{-}1\end{bmatrix}^{ op} egin{bmatrix} f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star})\ f(x^{k+1})-f(x^{\star}) \end{bmatrix} \[0.6em] ext{subject to} &x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k},\ &\lVert abla f(x^{k})-d^{k} Vert \leqslant\varepsilon\lVert abla f(x^{k}) Vert,\ & abla f(x^{\star})=0. \end{array} \end{equation*}

Here, \(f\) is an infinite-dimensional optimization variable, even though only its values and gradients at \(x^{k}\), \(x^{k+1}\), and \(x^{\star}\) appear in the objective and constraints. Introducing corresponding variables \(f^i\) and \(g^i\) therefore gives the equivalent formulation

egin{equation*} egin{array}{cl} \mathop{ ext{maximize}}\limits_{\substack{ x^{k},x^{k+1},x^{\star},d^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\ g^{k},g^{k+1},g^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\ f^{k},f^{k+1},f^{\star}\in\mathbb{R} }} & ext{trace}((S_+^{ op}QS_+- ho S^{ op}QS)\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star},g^{k},g^{k+1},d^{k})) +q egin{bmatrix}- ho\\phantom{-}1\end{bmatrix}^{ op} egin{bmatrix} f^{k}-f^{\star}\ f^{k+1}-f^{\star} \end{bmatrix} \[0.6em] ext{subject to} &x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k},\ &\lVert g^{k}-d^{k} Vert\leqslant\varepsilon\lVert g^{k} Vert,\ &g^{\star}=0,\ & ext{there exists }f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) \; ext{such that}\; f(x^i)=f^i\; ext{and}\; abla f(x^i)=g^i \; ext{for each}\; i\in\{k,k+1,\star\}. \end{array} \end{equation*}

At first glance, this may not seem like progress: we have replaced the infinite-dimensional variable by an existence constraint over the same function class. Have we actually made the problem any easier?

Determining whether the prescribed values and gradients can come from a single function in \(\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\) is an interpolation problem. For this class, interpolation conditions from the performance estimation literature let us replace the existence constraint by finitely many explicit inequalities [THG17]. The quadratic bounds \(\eqref{eq:quadratic-bounds}\), imposed only at the sampled points, are necessary but not sufficient for interpolation. Theorem 1 gives necessary and sufficient conditions for a function in \(\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\) to match all the prescribed values and gradients.

Theorem 1 (Smooth and strongly convex interpolation). [THG17, Theorem 4]

Let \(J\) be a finite index set, and let \(x^i,g^i\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) and \(f^i\in\mathbb{R}\) for each \(i\in J\). There exists a function \(f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\) satisfying

egin{equation*} f(x^i)=f^i\; ext{and}\; abla f(x^i)=g^i\; ext{for each}\; i\in J \end{equation*}

if and only if

egin{equation*} f^i-f^j-\inner{g^j}{x^i-x^j} \geqslant frac{\mu}{2} orm{x^i-x^j}^{2} + frac{1}{2(L-\mu)} orm{g^i-g^j-\mu(x^i-x^j)}^{2} \end{equation*}

for each pair of distinct indices \(i,j\in J\).

For an intuitive explanation of interpolation in the convex, possibly nonsmooth case, corresponding to \(\mu=0\) and \(L=+\infty\), see Adrien Taylor’s excellent post on Francis Bach’s blog [Tay20].

Applying Theorem 1 gives the following equivalent finite-dimensional formulation, where we have squared the relative-error bound and written each inequality with zero on the right

egin{equation*} egin{array}{cl} \mathop{ ext{maximize}}\limits_{\substack{ x^{k},x^{k+1},x^{\star},d^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\ g^{k},g^{k+1},g^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\ f^{k},f^{k+1},f^{\star}\in\mathbb{R} }} & ext{trace}((S_+^{ op}QS_+- ho S^{ op}QS)\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star},g^{k},g^{k+1},d^{k})) +q egin{bmatrix}- ho\\phantom{-}1\end{bmatrix}^{ op} egin{bmatrix} f^{k}-f^{\star}\ f^{k+1}-f^{\star} \end{bmatrix} \[0.6em] ext{subject to} &x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k},\ & orm{g^{k}-d^{k}}^{2}-\varepsilon^{2} orm{g^{k}}^{2}\leqslant0,\ &g^{\star}=0,\ &f^j-f^i+\inner{g^j}{x^i-x^j} + frac{\mu}{2} orm{x^i-x^j}^{2} + frac{1}{2(L-\mu)} orm{g^i-g^j-\mu(x^i-x^j)}^{2}\leqslant0\ & ext{for each pair of distinct indices }i,j\in\{k,k+1,\star\}. \end{array} \end{equation*}

We have now eliminated the unknown function: only finitely many vector and scalar variables remain. For the three indices in \(\{k,k+1,\star\}\), there are six interpolation inequalities: one for each ordered pair of distinct indices. Swapping \(i\) and \(j\) generally gives a different inequality.

Rewriting the constraints. Substituting \(x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k}\) and \(g^{\star}=0\) eliminates \(x^{k+1}\) and \(g^{\star}\) as optimization variables. The relative-error constraint becomes

egin{equation*} orm{g^{k}-d^{k}}^{2}-\varepsilon^{2} orm{g^{k}}^{2} = ext{trace}(A_{\mathrm{err}}\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star},g^{k},g^{k+1},d^{k})) \leqslant0, \qquad A_{\mathrm{err}}= egin{bmatrix} 0&\phantom{-}0&0&\phantom{-}0\ 0&\phantom{-}1-\varepsilon^{2}&0&-1\ 0&\phantom{-}0&0&\phantom{-}0\ 0&-1&0&\phantom{-}1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{equation*}

For each interpolation inequality, we use \(A_{i,j}\in\mathbb{S}^{4}\) to represent the inner products and squared norms and \(a_{i,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\) to select the function-value difference \(f^{j}-f^{i}\). The six inequalities can then be written as

egin{equation*} ext{trace}(A_{i,j}\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star},g^{k},g^{k+1},d^{k})) +a_{i,j}^{ op} egin{bmatrix} f^{k}-f^{\star}\ f^{k+1}-f^{\star} \end{bmatrix} \leqslant0 \end{equation*}

for each pair of distinct indices \(i,j\in\{k,k+1,\star\}\).

Show derivationHide derivation

For each of the six ordered pairs, we first write the interpolation inequality, then substitute \(x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k}\) and \(g^{\star}=0\), expand the squared norms, and identify its trace representation.

For \((i,j)=(k,\star)\), we obtain

egin{align*} &f^{\star}-f^{k}+\inner{g^{\star}}{x^{k}-x^{\star}} + frac{\mu}{2} orm{x^{k}-x^{\star}}^{2} + frac{1}{2(L-\mu)} orm{g^{k}-g^{\star}-\mu(x^{k}-x^{\star})}^{2}\ &=f^{\star}-f^{k} + frac{\mu}{2} orm{x^{k}-x^{\star}}^{2} + frac{1}{2(L-\mu)} orm{g^{k}-\mu(x^{k}-x^{\star})}^{2}\ &=f^{\star}-f^{k}+ frac{1}{2(L-\mu)}( \mu L orm{x^{k}-x^{\star}}^{2} -2\mu\inner{x^{k}-x^{\star}}{g^{k}} + orm{g^{k}}^{2})\ &= ext{trace}(A_{k,\star}\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star},g^{k},g^{k+1},d^{k})) +a_{k,\star}^{ op} egin{bmatrix}f^{k}-f^{\star}\f^{k+1}-f^{\star}\end{bmatrix}\leqslant0, \end{align*}

where

egin{equation*} A_{k,\star}= frac{1}{2(L-\mu)} egin{bmatrix} \phantom{-}\mu L&-\mu&0&0\ -\mu&\phantom{-}1&0&0\ \phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&0&0\ \phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&0&0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad a_{k,\star}= egin{bmatrix}-1\\phantom{-}0\end{bmatrix}. \end{equation*}

For \((i,j)=(\star,k)\), we obtain

3. Searching for Lyapunov functions

In Section 2, we compared the one-step contraction factors obtained from squared distance to the solution and function-value suboptimality. A contracting Lyapunov function that bounds a performance measure from above can certify a faster asymptotic rate than a direct contraction bound for that measure, or establish convergence even when the measure does not contract at every iteration. Here we search for such a Lyapunov function within a chosen family. We illustrate this search using stationary gradient methods with memory to solve \(\eqref{eq:optimization-problem}\), i.e., to minimize a function \(f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^d)\).

3.1 Stationary gradient methods with memory

Given constants \(\gamma>0\) and \(\alpha, eta\in\mathbb{R}\), and initial points \(x^{0},x^{-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\), consider

egin{equation} \label{eq:gradient-method-with-memory} \left[ egin{aligned} y^{k} &= x^{k}+\alpha(x^{k}-x^{k-1}),\ x^{k+1} &= x^{k}-\gamma abla f(y^{k})+ eta(x^{k}-x^{k-1}). \end{aligned} ight. \end{equation}

The method is called stationary because \(\gamma\), \(\alpha\), and \( eta\) are constant across iterations. In the table below, we give some standard choices of \(\gamma\), \(\alpha\), and \( eta\).

  1. Gradient method: Optimal constant step size for worst-case distance contraction on \(\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\) [Pol63, Theorem 6; Nes18, Theorem 2.1.15].

4. Going further

Both examples use semidefinite programming to combine valid inequalities into a Lyapunov certificate, either for a fixed Lyapunov function or while searching for one within a chosen family.

The theoretical framework in [UBTG25] extends these ideas beyond the contraction bounds considered here. It covers sublinear convergence guarantees and splitting methods, including proximal gradient and Douglas–Rachford.

AutoLyap, described in [UDGT+26], supports broader classes of optimization and inclusion problems, iteration-dependent methods and analyses, and richer families of Lyapunov functions. Users specify the problem class, method, and desired Lyapunov analysis through a high-level interface. The software constructs and numerically solves the corresponding SDPs. Its documentation provides worked examples.

entry.summary: Many convergence proofs for first-order methods in optimization follow a common pattern: construct a Lyapunov function, establish an inequality describing its decrease, and use this inequality to show that a performance measure converges to zero. Within many standard problem classes and prescribed families of Lyapunov functions, these tasks can often be formulated exactly as semidefinite programs (SDPs). Existing solvers can then be used to search numerically for feasible solutions. Convergence analysis itself thus becomes a tractable optimization problem.
